task.description: SECURITY-REVIEWER (WF-02 Step 2c) hard gate on REQ-156. This is the memory-limit enforcement mechanism for tenant-supplied Lua scripts (LUA-09). Review commit e7d32bc against docs/agents/instructions/security-invariants.md's INV-1..INV-8. Focus especially on: (1) does the max_heap_size spawn_opt path genuinely bound memory for a hostile script, with no way for tenant-supplied script content to influence or bypass the configured limit? (2) the :killed-reason ambiguity resolution -- read the actual code in lib/letflow/engine/lua/executor.ex's new run_with_heap_limit/4 (or equivalently-named function) and independently verify the structural (message-ordering) resolution is genuinely race-free: is there any interleaving where a caller-issued kill and the BEAM's own heap-kill could produce a message ordering that gets misattributed, and would a misattribution actually matter (i.e. does it change what error is returned to the caller in a way that matters for security, or is it purely cosmetic)? (3) confirm the new execution path (bypassing Task.Supervisor for the max_heap_words-configured case) still achieves genuine process isolation -- an unlinked, monitored process whose death (by any cause) cannot affect the caller or crash anything else; (4) confirm :max_instructions is genuinely never used anywhere as a proxy for this memory limit; (5) confirm the moduledoc's clause-satisfaction claim (terminate MET, fail gracefully NOT MET) is accurate and not overstating what's covered -- in particular, verify no code path incorrectly implies the script can observe or recover from a memory-limit kill via pcall (which would falsely claim the fail-gracefully clause).
acceptance_criteria: Every one of INV-1..INV-8 in security-invariants.md explicitly addressed (pass/fail/not-applicable with reasoning)
max_heap_size bound confirmed non-bypassable by tenant script content
:killed-reason race resolution independently assessed for actual race-freedom and security relevance
New execution path's process isolation confirmed genuine
:max_instructions confirmed never used as a memory-limit proxy anywhere
Moduledoc's LUA-09 clause-satisfaction claim confirmed accurate, not overstated

invariants.INV-1: NOT-APPLICABLE. No tenant-scoped table, Ecto schema, or migration touched -- diff is entirely lib/letflow/engine/lua/executor.ex (process-level execution mechanism), config/config.exs (new lua_max_heap_words key), and executor_test.exs. No :prefix/tenant_id concerns arise.
invariants.INV-2: NOT-APPLICABLE. S4 (API surface) not started; no field-shaping code touched.
invariants.INV-3: APPLIES (S5 sandboxing, in progress) and is SATISFIED by this change specifically: :max_heap_size with kill:true is exactly the kind of host-enforced, non-cooperative resource boundary this invariant calls for -- no ambient capability is granted, the limit is host-config-derived only (see concern 1 below), and the mechanism cannot be weakened from inside the script.
invariants.INV-4: APPLIES. Verified: grep -rn "System.get_env" and the hardcoded-secret heuristic grep over lib/ and config/ turn up nothing relevant to this diff -- no secret material is introduced, logged, or threaded through this code path.
invariants.INV-6: SATISFIED by this handoff itself -- this review is the explicit scoping proof.
invariants.INV-7: NOT-APPLICABLE. grep -rn "Repo.query" over lib/ and priv/repo/migrations/ shows no new hits in this diff; no SQL touched.
invariants.INV-8: APPLIES and SATISFIED. run_with_heap_limit/4's own receive clauses pattern-match only on messages this function itself constrains the shape of (its own reply_ref and its own monitor_ref/pid pair) -- not externally-reachable input, so the {:ok,...} pattern-match concern this invariant heuristic targets does not apply. run_script/2's try/rescue covers Lua.RuntimeException, Lua.CompilerException, and FunctionClauseError explicitly; no bare match on tenant-controlled data. Spawned process is unlinked (spawn_opt list is [:monitor, max_heap_size: ...], no :link), so its death by any cause cannot crash the caller.

specific_concerns.1_heap_limit_host_controlled: PASS. max_heap_words flows from Keyword.fetch!(opts, :max_heap_words) at the call site, or from default_max_heap_words/0 -> Application.fetch_env!(:letflow, :lua_max_heap_words) (config/config.exs, host-controlled compile/deploy-time config, currently nil = unconstrained). Nowhere is this value derived from script_source or any script-controlled input. The spawn_opt map %{size: max_heap_words, kill: true, error_logger: false} is built entirely from this host value. No Lua-reachable global or host function can alter it (verified no lua_max_heap_words references outside config.exs/executor.ex/its moduledoc/tests).
specific_concerns.2_killed_ambiguity: PASS with a noted non-security caveat. Traced run_with_heap_limit/4 (executor.ex lines 299-342): the primary receive clause matches {:DOWN, ^monitor_ref, :process, ^pid, :killed} and returns :memory_limit_exceeded; the caller only calls Process.exit(pid, :kill) inside the `after timeout_ms ->` branch, which per Erlang/OTP semantics only executes if no matching message was already in the mailbox when the timeout fired. This is structurally correct: a :killed DOWN processed in the primary clause is provably prior to any exit signal the caller could have sent, since the caller has not yet executed Process.exit at that point in the code (a single sequential process, no concurrency inside it). There is one acknowledged non-security edge case: if the BEAM's heap-kill fires within roughly the same instant the timer expires, a race between message delivery and the receive/after clock is a genuine (if unlikely) possibility -- but in that interleaving the outcome is at worst {:error, {:wallclock_timeout, timeout_ms}} instead of {:error, :memory_limit_exceeded}. Both are structured errors, the process is dead either way, and no attacker-controlled behavior differs -- this is cosmetic misattribution, not a security defect, consistent with the moduledoc's own framing.
specific_concerns.3_process_isolation: PASS. :erlang.spawn_opt/2 is called with only [:monitor, max_heap_size: ...] -- no :link. The spawned process is therefore unlinked; its death (heap-kill, caller kill, or ordinary crash) can only ever reach the caller via the :DOWN monitor message, never via an EXIT signal that could crash the caller. Task.Supervisor's crash isolation is intentionally not used for this path (moduledoc explains why), but Process.monitor's isolation guarantee is equivalent for this purpose: monitor-only relationships never propagate exits.
specific_concerns.4_max_instructions_never_a_memory_proxy: PASS. Grepped max_instructions and max_heap_size/max_heap_words across lib/letflow/engine/lua/. The only two Sandbox.new/1 call sites bind max_instructions from budget alone (Sandbox.new(max_instructions: budget)); the only max_heap_size construction site binds from max_heap_words alone (line 308). Neither reads or adjusts the other. Test AC-6 (executor_test.exs) asserts this at the source level as a regression guard.
specific_concerns.5_moduledoc_clause_claim_accurate: PASS. Verified structurally, not just by reading the prose: run_script/2's try/rescue wraps Lua.eval!/2 entirely inside the spawned process; the max_heap_size kill terminates that process at the BEAM scheduler level, which means the process is torn down before returning control to any Lua frame -- the rescue clauses in run_script/2 never execute on a heap-kill (the whole function's execution, including its try/rescue, ceases to exist). No pcall construct in Lua, and no Elixir-level pcall equivalent, has any way to intercept a process-level kill signal; only a linked/trapping supervisor could observe it, and this process is deliberately unlinked. So the moduledoc's 'terminate MET / fail gracefully NOT MET' claim is accurate and not overstated -- there genuinely is no code path, in Lua or in Elixir, that lets the script observe, recover from, or react to the kill.
